Three stops now. Father Anselm needs a witness, Ezra needs me to mind my business, and I'm walking past the college with no one here. The bakery shift doesn't open for another hour—Marta doesn't unlock before nine—and school, if there's anyone to teach, hasn't started.

Ezra said don't let it unsettle my day, but Anselm's already told me who he's watching. Hester Vance. The woman who remembers things the ledger writes differently. And he's doing it now, before the council election closes its candidacy at nine, before voting opens at noon.

*she begins walking, faster than before*

The ledger page. I read it. The boundary dispute—the Thornes' claim to the north field. Anselm's office wrote it down one way, Hester says it was another. If he's asking her about it now, when the council balance could shift...

*calls out as she walks through empty streets*

He's not looking for a witness. He's looking for which story holds. And if Hester Vance is the last one who saw the old stones moved, if she remembers where the markers stood before Wren Thorne's grandfather planted his first wheat—

*reaches the forge yard, breathing hard*

Two things. First: whether anyone's still here. Second: whether Father Anselm's going to the Vances, or whether he's already been.

*looks for the back door, where Kem usually stacks deliveries*

Ezra. You already know this isn't about an old man's memory. You were there when the boundary came up in office last spring. You said nothing, and I noticed. Still no one here. The college empties out when the real work begins—harvest, election, whatever pulls people away from books. But I need to know: did anyone see Anselm leave? Did he go toward the Vance house, or toward the government complex where candidates are still declaring?

*weighs the timing on her fingers*

Candidacy closes at nine. That's forty minutes. If he's moving against Hester's testimony before the council changes, he's running out of morning.

*decides, sharp*

The bakery's closer than the Vance house, and Marta Thorne sees more than she says. Also: I owe her the morning work whether school's empty or not. Two birds.

*walks with purpose, not running—running looks like fear*

If Anselm's at the Vances, I'll hear it from Hester or Junia or Aldous at lunch. If he's at the government complex, I'll see him when I check who's standing for council. Delia's already declared—that's my mother, running against Ainsley Holloway, and neither of them have said why the third seat matters enough to fight for it.

*reaches for the bakery door*

But first: flour, fire, and whether Marta knows why the office wants her family's boundary claim questioned before noon.  The bakery's warmth hits like a wall—Marta's ovens have been running since before dawn, and the smell of rye and something burning edges the air. I know that smell. She lets the crusts go dark when she's thinking.

*looks for her behind the counter, or in the back where the mixing happens*

Marta. The morning delivery came—Idris or Corwin must have dropped the flour before light. I can start on the round loaves, or whatever's short for the election crowd. They'll want bread by noon when they walk back from voting.

*pauses, watching the street door*

But first: has Father Anselm been by? He left the forge saying he needed a witness, and Hester Vance is the only one old enough for what he's chasing. If he's asked her about the north field already, if he's trying to get her story on record before the council changes—

*counts quietly, angry*

That's not history. That's timing. And I want to know who's doing it to us  Liora's here. And Bram Holloway's in the back with Marta, six turns of conversation already, no topic named—which means they're not saying it out loud where customers could hear.

I stood in the doorway of my own home and heard Ezra say he'd voted Delia's way. Seventeen years living here and I still didn't know which way that was—left or right, keep or change, Thorne or Vance or something else entirely. She never said. Neither of them did. The forge ran on what was needed for the work and what wasn't spoken at dinner.

"Ezra," I said, because he was standing there and had asked me something I hadn't answered. "My studies are fine. Aldous Vance is still lazier than me and still cleverer, and I still don't know which of us that will cost more."

But that wasn't the true thing, and I was too tired from the bakery to pretend otherwise.

"What I need you to actually tell me is—when you voted Delia's way, what was the way? Because I'm hearing Ainsley Holloway's name spoken in the same sentence as 'governs,' and I'm standing in rooms where people's grandmothers start testifying about silver claims that appeared convenient to whoever needed them to. You already know that I read the boundary page. I know the Thornes are in the right. But right doesn't govern unless someone puts it there."

I watched him. My father, who never said what he thought until the iron was ready. I was counting on that habit being a two-way door—if he wouldn't speak before knowing, he also wouldn't lie after.

"Nell Holloway moved the western marker. Perrin put his own coin in a jar to hide what he found empty. Ainsley stood in a doorway through all of it and still wants me to believe she 'set aside' 400 sim for a debt her own nephew says was already paid." I held up one finger, then two, then three. "That's three witnesses. Four if you count me, five if you count whoever told Ainsley which shelf held which jar—which means someone between Idris Thorne's eyes and Ainsley's instructions, because Idris doesn't work the office. He works the yard."

I let that sit. The forge was warm. Ezra would wait to see if the metal held.

"So when you say you voted Delia's way, what I'm actually asking is: did her way keep the people who manufacture debt and move markers? Or did it put someone in place who'll dig where the dirt is?"

I let the silence breathe around my father's question. He's asked three times, and I've heard him each time. He thinks this is about silver claims and council business.

He's wrong, and he's not the only one who needs to hear the answer.

I turn so my voice carries to both of them, Kem working the accounts by oil-light, Ezra at his bench with the iron still cooling.

"Ainsley Holloway." Another beat. "Hester Vance named me tonight, accused me of turning grandfather's assay toward silver claims. Except I never mentioned silver. Never asked about it, never read the land register for it, never breathed a word."

I set the bread down on the table between us. "Hester Vance attends me most evenings and never once mentioned silver. Neither of you ever mentioned it. Aldous Vance tried to buy my silence with a silver puzzle at the college this morning—asked what I'd do if I saw a mother 'neither desperate nor visible' in the claims that show silver."

My father's hands still on his work. Kem's pen stops scratching.

"You already know that I don't trade what I know," I continue. "And I didn't trade it tonight. But Ainsley Holloway knew about the empty assay jar before Perrin ever touched the office shelves. She knew which jar, which debt, which morning. And when I asked her directly—twenty turns in the bakery, three different ways—she never answered. She stood through Nell's confession and said nothing. Through Perrin's accusation and said nothing."

I look from one to the other. "The boundary page shows the Thornes are in the right. Wren's claim is valid, the western marker was moved. But someone at the office knew that before Anselm's inquiry started. Someone with keys to the storeroom, someone who weighs the receipts before they're written into the ledger."

"Delia governs now," my father repeats, but his voice has shifted. This isn't council business anymore. This is his household, his forge, his daughter standing in the middle of something that reaches toward us.

"It's not about the silver," I say. "It's about who knew what was in the jar before it was empty. Who knew the boundary page would favor the Thornes before the inquiry opened. Who's been standing in doorways listening while everyone else talks."

I let him work through it. Ezra Okonjo is slower than me but not stupid. The silence stretches until I count three on my fingers, angry-counting, the way I do when adults stall.

"Kem. You said you'd answer if Ainsley sends for you."

My brother looks up from his accounts. "I said I'd answer. I didn't say what I'd say."

"Tell her this. Tell her Tova Okonjo is at the forge. Tell her Tova Okonjo read the boundary page and knows the Thornes are in the right. Tell her Tova Okonjo noticed who stood silent through twenty turns of confession, and who tried to bury a debt that didn't exist."

I pick up the bread again. "And tell her if she wants to know what else I noticed, she can come explain why Hester Vance thinks I'm looking for silver when I never asked the question."
